extracted.intended_audience: English citizens and policymakers concerned with fiscal and social reform (late 18th century)
extracted.subtask_short: drafting progressive tax and welfare plan
extracted.subtask_description: A pamphlet-style plan proposing comprehensive social-welfare programs, specific cash allowances and pensions, and detailed progressive taxation to fund them and to reduce aristocratic influence and the national debt. Includes numerical proposals, tax-rate tables, and implementation notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abolition of two millions poor-rates
rubrics_metrics.description: Abolish two millions in poor-rates (relief of the poor-rates burden).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as the first item of the plan; abolition seen as foundational to relieve the poor and prevent the misery produced by parish poor laws. Funding implied from reallocation of tax receipts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision for two hundred and fifty-two thousand poor families
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide for 252,000 poor families, at the rate of four pounds per head for each child under fourteen years of age; additionally provide education for one million and thirty thousand children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies numbers and per-child amount; proposed to be funded from reallocated taxes. Tied to abolition of poor-rates and the aim of preventing ragged and hungry children and reducing petty crime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annuity of six pounds for age 50–60
rubrics_metrics.description: Grant an annuity of six pounds per annum each for poor persons, decayed tradesmen, and others (supposed seventy thousand) from age fifty until sixty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as part of a staged pension scheme to support aged/work-worn people before full old-age annuity begins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annuity of ten pounds for life from age 60
rubrics_metrics.description: Grant an annuity of ten pounds each for life for poor persons, decayed tradesmen, and others (supposed seventy thousand) from age sixty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complements the 6-pound annuity (50–60) to provide continuous life support for the aged poor; numbers and target population estimated in the plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Donation for births
rubrics_metrics.description: One-time donation of twenty shillings each for fifty thousand births.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A fixed grant to support new births; specified target count and amount.

rubrics_metrics.name: Donation for marriages
rubrics_metrics.description: One-time donation of twenty shillings each for twenty thousand marriages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A fixed grant to support marriages; specified target count and amount.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funeral allowance for travelling workers
rubrics_metrics.description: Allowance of twenty thousand pounds for the funeral expenses of persons travelling for work and dying at a distance from their friends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A lump-sum annual allowance to avoid burdensome costs and indignities when itinerant workers die away from home.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employment for casual poor in London and Westminster
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide employment, at all times, for the casual poor in the cities of London and Westminster.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A standing employment provision specifically targeted at urban casual poor to reduce vagrancy and destitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abolition of the tax on houses and windows
rubrics_metrics.description: Strike off (abolish) the tax on houses and windows, a direct tax that falls heavily on the middle class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantifies the tax (returns of 1788) and argues abolition will leave about one million surplus taxes; recommends keeping a reserve and not immediately extending reductions beyond certain items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowance to disbanded soldiers and officers
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose fifteen thousand soldiers to be disbanded and make an allowance of three shillings a week during life to each, paid like Chelsea College pensions; provide proportionate allowances to officers of disbanded corps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes arithmetic of annual costs (L117,000 for men, same for officers) and recommends treating disbanded navy similarly; aims to avoid making ex-soldiers sufferers when forces are reduced by alliances/peace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increase of pay to remaining soldiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Increase pay to the remaining soldiers by an additional fifteen thousand sixpences per week (annual L19,500).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of the military reorganization budget; accounted for in the half-million annual cost estimates for demobilization and pay increases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Same allowances and increases applied to navy
rubrics_metrics.description: Admit the same sums to be applied to the disbanded navy as to the army, and the same increase of pay to remaining naval personnel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit symmetry between army and navy in disbandment allowances and pay increases; doubles the calculated yearly cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abolition of the commutation tax
rubrics_metrics.description: Abolish the commutation tax (amount cited L771,657 in 1788 returns) and substitute a progressive tax on estates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues commutation tax is heavily felt and proposes replacing it to (1) move burden to those best able to bear it, (2) restore justice among families by property distribution, and (3) extirpate primogeniture and aristocratic electoral influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progressive tax on estates (Table I rates)
rubrics_metrics.description: Impose a progressive tax on all estates of clear yearly value above L50, with increasing rates per pound on each progressive thousand (explicit schedule given: 0s3d per pound up to L500; then 0s6d on L500–L1,000; then on successive thousands rates rise up to 20s in the pound by the twenty-third thousand).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Full table of per-pound rates per successive thousands presented (TABLE I). Purpose: make taxation more equal, and to reduce overconcentration of estates and the power of primogeniture. Author notes it may be lowered for smaller estates if it produces more than the commutation tax.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tax incidence examples and totals (Table II and III)
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed computation of what estates of various annual values would pay under the progressive tax (TABLE II and TABLE III show tax on each estate and net produce after tax for estates up to L23,000).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tables illustrate progressive tax burden and show that net produce plateaus (around L12,370 clear) to argue large estates lose profit incentive to remain undivided; used to justify likely descent of property to younger children.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of excise collections to fund reforms
rubrics_metrics.description: Fund the plan by changing the application of existing taxes and drawing money from excise collections, which are made eight times a year in every market town in England.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims plan is easy in practice and will not embarrass trade because it reallocates existing collections rather than creating sudden new taxes; suggests this as immediate funding source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep a reserve and phase reductions
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain a sum in reserve for incidental matters and avoid extending tax reductions too far in the first instance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After striking off certain taxes, recommends retaining about one million surplus as a reserve and using additional modes of reform rather than immediate further reductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progressive taxation to counter primogeniture and aristocratic influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Use progressive taxation not merely to raise revenue but to 'extirpate the overgrown influence arising from the unnatural law of primogeniture' by making very large estates less profitable and encouraging division among heirs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The progressive tax is explicitly positioned as a political and social instrument to restore equilibrium and reduce aristocratic domination of elections and public life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improve salaries of inferior revenue-officers
rubrics_metrics.description: Raise salaries of inferior revenue-officers (many under fifty pounds a year) to a decent level (suggested seventy pounds), requiring about one hundred and twenty thousand pounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues it's a reproach that revenue is wasted in sinecures while hardworking officers get petty pittance; proposes targeted modest increases to restore decency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address inferior clergy incomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Rectify large disparities in clergy incomes (some with twenty or thirty pounds a year versus others with ten thousand) as a matter of common justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentioned as another class deserving attention; author refrains from extensive discussion but raises it as a justice claim irrespective of denominational partialities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize reforms in current expenses over interest payments
rubrics_metrics.description: Make tax reforms in the current expenses of government rather than by touching monies applied to the interest of the national debt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that relieving poor taxes and striking off certain taxes will more directly relieve the people; contends that reducing the capital of the debt does not benefit the public unless it reduces the annual interest burden (taxes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tax interest on the national debt progressively to extinguish it
rubrics_metrics.description: Propose taxing the interest on government stock (the national debt) by a small progressive duty (e.g., one halfpenny in the pound first year, a penny second year, etc.), applying the proceeds to reduce the debt and concurrently lowering other taxes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains mechanism: tax collected at payment time with no collection expense; demonstrates small initial rates could replace specific small taxes (e.g., wagon tax) and be applied progressively so that stockholders pay less overall when reliefs are included. Emphasizes gradual, self-applying process and political pragmatism (stockholders would gain popularity/security).

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply surplus taxes to reduce certain excises gradually
rubrics_metrics.description: As demobilization sums 'fall in' annually, use the reductions to remove or lessen particular duties (e.g., when thirty thousand pounds falls in remove hop duty; later lessen duties on candles and soap) until they cease.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives an implementation timeline principle: as annuity/levy items expire, translate the freed funds to eliminate regressive excises; the approach is gradual to avoid disruption and create sustainable relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of taxing 'luxury' as excessive property
rubrics_metrics.description: Argues 'luxury' should be judged by amount/means (excess wealth), not item, so overgrown estates are proper objects of taxation; suggests a threshold (e.g., first L1,000 necessary, subsequent thousands increasingly luxury) and that prohibition (very high rates) should be placed beyond probable industry acquisition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as normative justification for progressive estate taxation and for limiting accumulation by bequest (primogeniture); warns against setting arbitrary bounds on property from industry but defends limits on bequest accumulation.
